pages.alt: Lesson 3's arm, length 1, turned 360° anticlockwise from pointing right. Its tip's height, 0, is carried level across to a graph of height against time, where a pen has drawn the wave so far.
pages.name: The arm draws a wave
pages.text: Here is lesson 3's arm again, length 1, pointing right. Set it turning anticlockwise at a steady speed. A dashed line carries its tip's height across to a graph, and a pen there draws that height as time goes on. The arm turns steadily, so its angle grows in step with time, and the graph is `sin θ` drawn against time. It rises to 1 at a quarter turn, is back at 0 at a half turn, falls to −1 at three quarters and is 0 again at a full turn. Drag the tip, or pause it to read the height.

pages.why: The trace follows the tip's height, the sine. At a half turn the tip sits on the across axis, so its height is `sin 180° = 0`. The −1 is its across shadow, `cos 180°`, which this trace does not draw.

pages.text: Now make the arm 10 long. An arm of length E is lesson 3's picture drawn E times bigger, so its tip's height is `E sin θ`. Turning once, it draws the same wave ten times as tall, up to 10 at a quarter turn and down to −10 at three quarters. The wave's highest point is the arm's length, its [[amplitude]]. Slide the arm's length and watch the wave grow and shrink with it.

pages.task: An arm of length 4 is frozen at 30°. How high is its tip?
pages.why: The height is the length times the sine: `4 × sin 30° = 4 × 0.5 = 2`. The 3.46 is `4 × cos 30°`, the across shadow, and 0.5 is `sin 30°` alone, the height of an arm of length 1.

pages.alt: The arm turning 2 times a second on a graph one second wide: 2 whole waves fill the second, and each wave, one turn, takes 0.5 s, the period.
pages.name: Turns a second
pages.text: Now turn the arm 2 times a second, on a graph one second wide. Each turn draws one whole wave, so two waves fill the second. The turns a second are the waves a second, the [[frequency]], counted in hertz (Hz), and the time one wave takes is the [[period]], here half a second. Slide the turns a second and watch more waves squeeze into the same second, each one shorter.

pages.alt: A wave that repeats every 10 ms: two waves across 20 ms, one turn of the arm each.
pages.name: Every 10 ms
pages.task: A wave repeats every 10 ms. What is its frequency?
pages.why: 10 ms is 0.01 s, so `1 ÷ 0.01 = 100` waves fit in a second: 100 Hz. The 0.01 is the period itself, the time one wave takes, and 10 counts milliseconds, not waves.

pages.text: Radians count the same turning in radius-lengths, as in lesson 5: one turn, 360°, is 2π radians. So f turns a second is 2πf radians a second, the arm's [[angular speed]], ω. After t seconds the arm has turned ωt radians from pointing right, so its height is `E sin(ωt) = E sin(2πft)`. At 50 Hz, `ω = 2π × 50 = 314.16` rad/s; at 60 Hz, common on ships, `ω = 2π × 60 = 376.99` rad/s, a wave every 16.7 ms. Because ωt is in radians, the calculator goes in radian mode. Slide the turns a second and watch ω follow.

pages.alt: The wave v = 10 sin(100πt), two turns of an arm of length 10. Each wave takes 20 ms.
pages.name: Read the frequency
pages.task: A wave is v = 10 sin(100πt). What is its frequency?
pages.why: The number in front of t is ω, here 100π radians a second. Each turn is 2π radians, so `f = 100π ÷ 2π = 50` turns a second, 50 Hz. 314.2 is ω itself, and 100 forgets the 2 in 2π.

pages.alt: Arm A starts pointing right and arm B 90° further round; both turn together, 50 times a second. B's wave is A's slid left by 5 ms.
pages.name: A head start
pages.text: Now add a second arm. Arm A starts pointing right, as before. Arm B starts a quarter turn on, at π/2 or 90°, and both turn together. B is already at the top at t = 0, so it reaches every height a quarter of a turn's time sooner. Its wave is A's slid left by a quarter period, 5 ms at 50 Hz. The start angle is the wave's [[phase]], φ, and B's wave is `E sin(ωt + φ)`. Slide φ below 0 and B starts behind: its wave slides right, later. Flip the switch to trace A's across shadow: at 90° it draws exactly B's wave, the [[cosine]] wave.

pages.alt: Arm A starts pointing right and arm B a quarter turn behind, pointing down, both the same length. Wave A is drawn, and wave B, slid right a quarter period.
pages.name: Wave B
pages.task: Wave A comes from an arm started pointing right. Arm B starts π/2 behind it. What is wave B?
pages.why: B is always a quarter turn behind A, so it reaches every height a quarter period later: its wave is A's slid right. It starts at the bottom, where A only gets after three quarters of a turn. Both arms are the same length, so the waves are just as tall.

pages.alt: The wave 10 sin(100πt) over 40 ms, and a level line at 5 meeting it 4 times, twice in each wave between the peaks.
pages.name: A level line
pages.text: Take the wave `10 sin(100πt)` and draw a level line at 5. It lies between the peaks, so it meets each wave twice, as lesson 3's level line met the circle twice. To find when, divide the height by 10, take sin⁻¹ in radian mode, find the other angle with the same sine, π minus the first, and divide each angle by ω, since the arm's angle is ωt. The rows under the picture work it through. Drag the level line up and down.

pages.alt: The wave 10 sin(100πt) and a level line at −8.3. Its first crossing is at 13.1 ms.
pages.name: A line at −8.3
pages.task: The line is now at −8.3. When does the wave 10 sin(100πt) first reach it?
pages.why: `sin⁻¹(−0.83) = −0.979`. Below the axis the arm is past the half turn, so it first gets there at `π + 0.979 = 4.121` radians, and `4.121 ÷ 314.16 = 13.1` ms. Dropping the minus gives 3.1 ms, when the wave is at +8.3, and the other angle, `2π − 0.979 = 5.304`, gives 16.9 ms, the second crossing.

pages.alt: The arm turned 360°, with its across shadow and height. The graph traces its slope, tan θ, against the angle, cut off at 4 and −4, with no value at 90° and 270°.
pages.name: The slope's graph
pages.text: Now trace the arm's slope instead of its height, `tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ` from Round the circle, against the angle. It is 0 at 0° and 1 at 45°, then climbs without limit as the arm nears straight up, so the graph is cut off at 4 and −4. At 90° and 270° the across shadow is 0, so the slope has no value there. Half a turn on, the arm points the opposite way: both shadows change sign, and their ratio stays the same. So tan repeats every half turn. Drag the tip.

pages.task: The arm is frozen at 135°, up and to the left. Is tan 135° positive or negative?
pages.why: At 135° the height is `sin 135° = 0.707`, and the across shadow points left, `cos 135° = −0.707`. So `tan 135° = 0.707 ÷ −0.707 = −1`, negative. tan has no value only at 90° and 270°, where the across shadow is 0.

pages.alt: A supply wave peaking at 325 V, 50 waves a second, two waves across 40 ms. Its wave is v = 325 sin(314.2t).
pages.name: A 50 Hz supply
pages.task: A supply peaks at 325 V at 50 Hz. Which is its wave?
pages.why: The number in front of t is ω, the radians a second: `ω = 2π × 50 = 314.2` rad/s, so `v = 325 sin(314.2t)`. With 50 there, the arm would turn only `50 ÷ 2π = 7.96` times a second, and 100 leaves out the π in 100π.

pages.alt: The wave v = 20 sin(ωt + π/2). At t = 0 the arm points straight up, a quarter turn on, and v = 20.
pages.name: Where it starts
pages.task: A wave is v = 20 sin(ωt + π/2). At t = 0, what is v?
pages.why: At t = 0 the bracket is just π/2, so the arm starts a quarter turn on, straight up, and `v = 20 sin(π/2) = 20 × 1 = 20`. 0 leaves out the phase, and 1 is `sin(π/2)` without the length 20.
